# 2 Samuel Chapter 19 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 190r–191r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_019_page_001.jpg, 2SA_019_page_002.jpg, 2SA_019_page_003.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** And it was told to Joab, "The king is weeping and mourning for Absalom."

**2** So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard it said that day, "The king is grieving for his son."

**3** The people stole into the city that day as soldiers steal in who are ashamed when they flee in battle.

**4** The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, "O my son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!"

**5** Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, "Today you have put to shame the faces of all your servants who saved your life this day, and the lives of your sons and daughters, and the lives of your wives and your concubines,

**6** because you love those who hate you and hate those who love you. You have made it clear today that commanders and servants are nothing to you. For I know this day that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, you would be pleased.

**7** Now arise, go out, and speak to the heart of your servants. For I swear by the LORD, if you do not go out, not a man will stay with you tonight. And that will be worse for you than all the evil that has come upon you from your youth until now."

**8** Then the king arose and sat in the gate. And when all the people were told, "The king is sitting in the gate," they all came before the king. Now Israel had fled, every man to his tent.

**9** All the people were arguing throughout the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies and saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled from the land because of Absalom.

**10** But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has died in battle. Why then do you say nothing about bringing the king back?"

**11** And King David sent word to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Speak to the elders of Judah, saying, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when the word of all Israel has come to the king?

**12** You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why should you be the last to bring back the king?'

**13** And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my bone and my flesh? God do so to me and more also, if you are not commander of the army before me from this day on, in place of Joab.'"

**14** And he turned the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, and they sent word to the king: "Return, you and all your servants."

**15** So the king returned and came to the Jordan. And Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and to escort him across the Jordan.

**16** Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.

**17** A thousand men of Benjamin were with him, along with Ziba, the servant of the house of Saul, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They rushed to the Jordan ahead of the king.

**18** They crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do whatever he thought good. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king as he was about to cross the Jordan.

**19** He said to the king, "Let not my lord hold me guilty, and do not remember how your servant acted perversely on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Let not the king take it to heart.

**20** For your servant knows that I have sinned. Behold, I have come this day, the first of all the house of Joseph, to come down and meet my lord the king."

**21** Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered, "Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the anointed of the LORD?"

**22** But David said, "What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah, that you should be an adversary to me this day? Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? Do I not know that today I am again king over Israel?"

**23** And the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king gave him his oath.

**24** Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had not tended his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his garments, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in peace.

**25** When he came from Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"

**26** He answered, "My lord, O king, my servant deceived me. For your servant said, 'I will saddle a donkey for myself, that I may ride on it and go with the king.' For your servant is lame.

**27** He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God; do therefore what is good in your eyes.

**28** For all my father's house were but men of death before my lord the king, yet you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What right have I still to cry out to the king?"

**29** The king said to him, "Why do you speak any more of your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the land."

**30** Mephibosheth said to the king, "Let him take it all, since my lord the king has come back safely to his own house."

**31** Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim and crossed with the king to the Jordan, to see him on his way.

**32** Barzillai was very old, eighty years of age. He had provided for the king during his stay at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man.

**33** The king said to Barzillai, "Come across with me, and I will provide for you in Jerusalem."

**34** But Barzillai said to the king, "How many are the days of the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?

**35** I am eighty years old today. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still hear the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?

**36** Your servant will go just a little way across the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?

**37** Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city, near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham — let him cross with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you."

**38** The king answered, "Chimham shall cross with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you. And whatever you ask of me, I will do for you."

**39** Then all the people crossed the Jordan, and the king crossed over. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home.

**40** The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went with him. All the people of Judah brought the king across, and also half the people of Israel.

**41** Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said, "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan, and all David's men with him?"

**42** All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close kinsman. Why are you angry over this? Have we eaten at all at the king's expense? Has he given us any gift?"

**43** The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David we have more than you. Why then did you treat us with contempt? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

This long and pivotal chapter moves through five major scenes: Joab's rebuke of the grieving king (vv.1–8), the political maneuvering to bring David home (vv.9–15), the three encounters at the Jordan — Shimei (vv.16–23), Mephibosheth (vv.24–30), and Barzillai (vv.31–39) — and the Judah-Israel dispute (vv.40–43). All three translators preserve the narrative structure faithfully. The chief translation challenges are Joab's harsh rhetoric (v.6), the mourning signs of Mephibosheth (v.24), Barzillai's meditation on aging (v.35), and the politically charged dispute of vv.41–43.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.3 — "stole into" vs. "slipped back into" vs. "stole away to come to"
- **EMET:** "stole-away to-come to-the-city"
- **LOGOS:** "stole into the city"
- **PNEUMA:** "slipped back into the city"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "stole into the city." The hitpael *vayyitgannev* means to move furtively; LOGOS is most concise and captures the shame.

---

### V.6 — "commanders and servants are nothing to you" vs. "officers and soldiers mean nothing to you"
- **EMET:** "nothing [are]-to-you commanders and-servants"
- **LOGOS:** "commanders and servants are nothing to you"
- **PNEUMA:** "your officers and soldiers mean nothing to you"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "commanders and servants are nothing to you." LOGOS preserves the Hebrew word pair (*sarim va-avadim*) accurately; PNEUMA's "officers and soldiers" modernizes unnecessarily.

---

### V.13 — "bone and flesh" vs. "flesh and blood"
- **EMET:** "my-bone and-my-flesh"
- **LOGOS:** "my bone and my flesh"
- **PNEUMA:** "my own flesh and blood"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "my bone and my flesh." The Hebrew *atsmi u-vesari* specifically says "bone and flesh," not "flesh and blood." PNEUMA's idiom is familiar but inaccurate.

---

### V.22 — "adversary" vs. "enemy"
- **EMET:** "as-an-adversary [le-satan]"
- **LOGOS:** "an adversary"
- **PNEUMA:** "my enemy"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "an adversary." The Hebrew *le-satan* uses the common noun meaning "opponent/accuser." LOGOS's "adversary" preserves the legal/political nuance without the personal tone of PNEUMA's "my enemy."

---

### V.24 — "tended his feet" vs. "done his feet" vs. "washed his feet"
- **EMET:** "had-not done his-feet [lo-asah raglav]"
- **LOGOS:** "had not tended his feet"
- **PNEUMA:** "had not washed his feet"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "had not tended his feet." The Hebrew *lo-asah raglav* is deliberately euphemistic — "had not done/made his feet." LOGOS's "tended" captures the grooming sense without specifying a single act (PNEUMA's "washed" is too narrow).

---

### V.24 — "beard" vs. "mustache"
- **EMET:** "his-mustache [sephamo]"
- **LOGOS:** "his beard"
- **PNEUMA:** "his beard"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "his beard." The Hebrew *sapham* refers specifically to the upper lip/mustache area, but English "beard" encompasses facial hair generally and is the conventional rendering.

---

### V.35 — "Can I discern between good and evil?" vs. "Can I tell the difference?"
- **EMET:** "Can-I-discern between good and-evil [ben tov le-ra']?"
- **LOGOS:** "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?"
- **PNEUMA:** "I can barely tell the difference between what tastes good and what doesn't"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" LOGOS rightly interprets *tov/ra'* in this context as pleasant/unpleasant (referring to taste and sensory experience) rather than moral categories. PNEUMA's rendering is too colloquial for this dignified speech.

---

### V.42 — "close kinsman" vs. "near" vs. "close relative"
- **EMET:** "near [qarov] [is] the-king to-us"
- **LOGOS:** "the king is our close kinsman"
- **PNEUMA:** "the king is our close relative"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the king is our close kinsman." LOGOS's "kinsman" carries the biblical resonance of tribal kinship better than PNEUMA's generic "relative."

---

### V.43 — "ten shares" vs. "ten portions"
- **EMET:** "ten portions [yadot]"
- **LOGOS:** "ten shares"
- **PNEUMA:** "ten shares"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "ten shares." The Hebrew *eser yadot* (literally "ten hands") means ten portions or shares. "Shares" is more idiomatic in English for political claims.

---

### V.43 — "fiercer" vs. "harder" vs. "more harsh"
- **EMET:** "harder [was the]-word"
- **LOGOS:** "fiercer"
- **PNEUMA:** "even more harsh"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "fiercer." The Hebrew *qashah* means hard/harsh/fierce. LOGOS's "fiercer" captures the escalating hostility that will erupt into revolt in chapter 20.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
